note: Feedback for the Checks of Unit 2. The design is docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-26-chemstudy-us-english-and-unit-1-check-feedback-design.md. Options are listed in the order they are to have on the page; the option with no message is the answer.

options.message: Electronegativity rises as you move across a period. Sulfur is not the farthest right of these four.
Electronegativity rises across a period and falls down a group. Selenium is neither the farthest right nor the highest up of these.
Bromine is far to the right, but electronegativity also falls as you move down a group.

options.text: The carbon atom is partly negative.
options.message: If either atom is partly negative, it is the one that pulls the shared pair harder. Compare the two electronegativities.

options.text: The oxygen atom is partly negative.
Neither atom carries a partial charge.
options.message: Even sharing takes the same, or nearly the same, electronegativity. Carbon and oxygen differ by 0.8.

options.text: The oxygen atom carries a full −1 charge.
options.message: A full charge means an electron was handed over, as in an ionic bond. In a C–O bond the pair is still shared.
A metal conducts while it is still solid. This solid does not.

options.text: Covalent bonds within molecules, with the molecules held by weak attractions
options.message: A solid made of molecules usually melts at a lower temperature, and it does not conduct even when melted.
The behavior is the evidence. Match the melting point and the two conduction tests against each kind of solid.
Ionic character grows with the difference in electronegativity. C and H differ by 0.4, so little that the bond is treated as nonpolar.
Nitrogen and oxygen are neighbors in one period, so their electronegativities are close. Look for the biggest difference.
Two atoms of the same element pull equally hard, so the difference is 0. Ionic character grows with the difference.
Zero is the energy of the atoms when they are far apart. Ask instead where two bonded atoms settle.
The steep part is where the nuclei are pushed too close and repel. The atoms do not stay there.

options.text: At the far right, where the curve levels off
options.message: At the far right the atoms are far apart and do not interact. That is not a bond.

options.text: At the lowest point of the curve

options.message: A single bond shares one pair. What does sharing more pairs do to the distance between the nuclei?
Bond order sets the length. Compare the number of shared pairs in each of the three bonds.

options.text: All three are the same length
options.message: The same two atoms can sit at different distances. The number of shared pairs changes how tightly the nuclei are held.
K⁺ and Br⁻ are large ions, so their centers stay far apart. And before sizes, compare the charges of the ions in each compound.
Look at the charges of the ions in each compound before you compare sizes. A change in charge usually matters more.
Small ions help, but size is the second thing to compare. Write the charge of each ion in all four compounds first.
Larger ions keep their centers farther apart. What does Coulomb's law say more distance does to the attraction?

options.text: MgO, because magnesium ions carry a larger charge than calcium ions
options.message: Check the charges: Mg²⁺ and Ca²⁺ are both 2+. Something other than charge has to decide.

options.text: They are the same, because the charges are the same
options.message: The charges tie, but charge is one of two things in Coulomb's law. Compare the distances between the ions' centers.
An ionic solid has no molecules. Its formula gives the ratio of the ions in the crystal.

options.text: Ions cannot move even in a liquid.
options.message: Ions are free to move in the liquid, which is why melted salt conducts. Ask what holds them in place in the solid.

options.text: Their covalent bonds must be broken to melt them.
options.message: The particles of an ionic solid are ions, and no shared pair joins one ion to the next. Ask what melting has to do to those ions.

options.text: Melting requires overcoming strong attractions between many oppositely charged ions.
The hammer breaks the covalent bonds inside the crystal.
options.message: Potassium chloride is made of K⁺ and Cl⁻ ions. There are no covalent bonds in the crystal to break.

options.text: The ions are pushed so close together that they turn into atoms.
options.message: A blow does not turn ions into atoms; they stay ions. Ask what the blow does to the pattern of charges in the crystal.

options.text: A shifted layer puts ions of the same charge next to each other, and they repel.
The delocalized electrons are knocked out of the crystal.
options.message: Delocalized electrons belong to metals. An ionic crystal is made of ions locked in place.
A current needs charges that can move. In the solid, every ion is locked in place by its neighbors.

options.text: Only when melted or dissolved in water.

options.message: A current needs charges that can move. Check whether the ions can move in each state.

options.text: Never, because it contains no free electrons.
options.message: Electrons are not the only charges that can carry a current. Ions can too, when they are free to move.

options.text: Copper atoms are smaller than sodium ions
options.message: The size of the particles does not decide whether a solid conducts. A current needs charges that can move.

options.text: Copper has stronger bonds than sodium chloride
options.message: How strong the bonds are does not decide whether a solid conducts. Ask which charges can move.

options.text: Copper's valence electrons are delocalized and free to move, while the ions in solid sodium chloride are fixed in place
Sodium chloride contains no charged particles
options.message: Sodium chloride is made of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions, so it is full of charge. Ask whether that charge can move in the solid.
A substitutional alloy forms from atoms of similar size. Compare 60 pm with 140 pm.
An alloy is a metal mixed with another element, and it still has its sea of electrons. Compare the two radii to see how the atoms fit.
Atoms of a different size can still fit into a metal's lattice. Compare the two radii to see where they would go.

options.text: It bends more easily, because carbon adds electrons to the sea
options.message: The sea of electrons is not what changes here. Ask how a metal bends, and what atoms of another size do to that.

options.text: It behaves the same, because carbon atoms are so small
options.message: Small atoms still take up room in the lattice. Ask how a metal bends, and whether atoms of another size change that.

options.text: It shatters, because carbon makes it ionic
options.message: Steel is still a metal, with its sea of electrons, so it is not ionic. Ask how a metal bends, and what the added carbon does to that.

options.text: It is harder to bend, because carbon atoms in the gaps keep the iron layers from sliding

slips.message: That is what the neutral atoms give. Did you count the charge of the ion?

slips.from: two electrons taken away for the 2− charge
slips.message: Did you take two electrons away for the charge? A negative ion has gained electrons.
That is what one sulfur and one oxygen give, with the charge. Check the subscript on the oxygen.

slips.from: every electron counted, not the valence electrons
slips.message: That is what counting every electron in the ion gives. A Lewis diagram counts valence electrons only.

options.text: H–C≡N, with one lone pair on N
H–C=N, with two lone pairs on N
options.message: Count the electrons around carbon in this diagram. Both electrons of every bond it is part of count for it.
Count the electrons drawn in this diagram, and compare with the count of valence electrons. Each one has to be somewhere.

options.text: H–C–N, with three lone pairs on N
options.message: Count the electrons around carbon in this diagram. With two single bonds it is well short of eight.
Count the valence electrons, then take away the ones used in the N–H bonds. Any left over go on nitrogen.
Two lone pairs and three bonds would put ten electrons around nitrogen. A second-period atom never holds more than eight.
Three lone pairs and three bonds would put twelve electrons around nitrogen. Compare that with the count of valence electrons.

options.text: The 2− charge was not counted, and it adds two electrons.
Oxygen was counted with 5 valence electrons instead of 6.
options.message: Try it: with 5 for each oxygen, the atoms would give 4 + 3 × 5 = 19, not 22. Oxygen is in group 16, so 6 is its number.

options.text: Carbon should have been given an expanded octet.
options.message: Carbon is in the second period, so it never holds more than eight. The fault here is in the count, not in the drawing.

options.text: A carbonate ion has 22 electrons, so nothing went wrong.
options.message: Do the count yourself from the formula, CO₃²⁻. Does every part of the formula appear in your sum?
Count around nitrogen: three bonds and one lone pair, with both electrons of each bond counted.
Count around carbon: four bonds, with both electrons of each bond counted.
Count around oxygen: two bonds and two lone pairs, with both electrons of each bond counted.
A single diagram puts the double bond on one oxygen atom. Could it just as well go on another?
Draw each structure out. Have you tried the double bond in every place it could go?
Resonance structures keep every atom in place and move only electron pairs. Count the places the double bond can go.
That is the order of a single bond in one diagram. The real ion is the average of all its resonance structures.
That is ozone's value: three bonding pairs spread over two bonds. Count the bonding pairs and the bonds in carbonate.
That is the order of the double bond in one diagram. The real ion is the average of all its resonance structures.

options.text: H–C≡N, with one lone pair on N
H–N≡C, with one lone pair on C
options.message: Work out the formal charge on N and on C in this arrangement: valence electrons minus nonbonding electrons minus bonds.
Check each arrangement atom by atom. Carbon and nitrogen bring different numbers of valence electrons, so swapping them changes the result.
Work out each atom's formal charge: valence electrons minus nonbonding electrons minus bonds. A triple bond counts 3.
Use the formula: valence electrons minus nonbonding electrons minus bonds. Count nitrogen's bonds and lone pairs in this ion, not in NH₃.
Check the order of the subtraction. Start from nitrogen's valence electrons, then take away its nonbonding electrons and its bonds.
That is the number of bonds. Formal charge starts from the valence electrons and takes the nonbonding electrons and the bonds away.

options.text: Nitrogen is in the second period.
options.message: Being in the second period keeps an atom from holding more than eight. It does not keep it from reaching eight.

options.text: Oxygen is more electronegative than nitrogen.
options.message: Electronegativity helps decide where a formal charge goes. It does not decide whether every atom can reach eight.

options.text: The molecule has an odd number of valence electrons, 17.

options.message: Ozone and the nitrate ion have resonance structures too, and every atom in them has eight. Resonance is not what leaves an atom short.
The Lewis diagram is drawn flat, so its angles mean nothing. Count all the domains on sulfur, lone pairs included.
A trigonal pyramidal shape has three bonds and one lone pair. Count the bonds on sulfur.
That is the electron geometry. The molecular shape is named from the positions of the atoms only.
Tetrahedral goes with four domains. Xenon has six here, and the lone pairs take up positions too.
Seesaw comes from five domains: four bonds and one lone pair. Xenon has six domains here.
That is the electron geometry for six domains. The shape is named from the atoms only, and two of the domains are lone pairs.
Its bonds are polar, but they point in opposite directions along a straight line. What do the two dipoles do?
It is trigonal planar, with three identical outer atoms spread evenly. Check whether its bond dipoles cancel.
It is tetrahedral, with four identical outer atoms spread evenly. Check whether its bond dipoles cancel.

slips.from: every line in O=C=O counted, σ and π together
slips.message: That is what counting every line in O=C=O gives. Some of those lines are σ bonds.
Did you count one double bond? Draw the Lewis diagram of CO₂ and count them.
Did you draw CO₂ with single bonds? Carbon would have fewer than eight electrons around it.

options.message: sp goes with two domains. Count the domains on one carbon: its bonds to hydrogen and its bond to the other carbon.
Did you count the double bond as two domains? Any bond, single, double or triple, is one domain.

options.text: It cannot be told without the shape.
options.message: Hybridization follows from the number of domains on the atom, and the Lewis diagram gives you that.
